segments.say: What actually happens when a deep assumption breaks? Janoff-Bulman, in her book Shattered Assumptions, published in 1992, described it vividly. She argued that a traumatic event doesn't just cause pain. It collides with our beliefs about the world, and forces us to face something we have always avoided: our own vulnerability, and the possibility that life is random.

In her account, the distress that follows is not only about the event itself. It's about the sudden loss of the framework that made the event unthinkable. The person is left with a world that no longer makes sense, and a self that no longer feels safe. That, she argued, helps explain why trauma feels so disorienting, even when the person is physically safe.

She proposed that the process of recovery involves rebuilding the assumptive world, and she distinguished between assimilation, in which people try to fit the new event into their old beliefs, and accommodation, in which the beliefs themselves change. Both can be part of the path, and which one dominates varies from person to person.

show.where: Shattered Assumptions: Towards a New Psychology of Trauma, 1992
show.what: The three core assumptions and what happens when trauma shatters them

segments.say: The terms come from the work of the developmental psychologist Jean Piaget, who used them for how children learn. Janoff-Bulman applied them to adults who face something that doesn't fit. A person can protect an old belief by bending the story, or they can bend the belief. The second is harder, and often the more lasting.

show.title: Two ways of making sense
items: Assimilation: fitting the event into old beliefs
Accommodation: changing the beliefs to fit the event
Accommodation can mean a more realistic worldview

segments.say: The theory was influential, and it also invited testing. If it's right, then people who've been through trauma should show shaken assumptions, and the more shaken the assumptions, the greater the distress. Several studies tested this idea, with mixed but interesting results.

In their work, Janoff-Bulman and Cynthia Frantz found that people who had experienced traumatic events often reported weaker beliefs in a benevolent world and a worthy self than people who hadn't. They suggested that the way people found meaning afterwards, either by making sense of what happened or by finding significance in life afterwards, was important in recovery.

show.where: The Transformation of Meaning in Psychological Therapies, 1997
show.what: The impact of trauma on meaning: from meaningless world to meaningful life

segments.say: Later reviews of this research found some support for the idea that traumatic experiences can be associated with changed beliefs about the world and the self, especially for events that involve human harm, such as violence or betrayal. They also found that the picture is more complicated than a single shattering. Many people hold on to much of their view, and some change in ways that are not uniformly negative.

The last two lines matter. A popular version of the theory suggests that trauma smashes the assumptive world in everyone. The research suggests that this is too simple. Beliefs can bend, flex or hold. The degree depends on the person, the event, and what happens next.

show.title: What reviews suggest
items: Trauma can change beliefs about safety and trust
Human-caused events tend to shake beliefs more

segments.say: It's easy to think that this only applies to dramatic events. But the same process, on a smaller scale, happens with many life changes: a divorce, a job loss, the end of a faith, the death of an older parent, a betrayal by a friend. In each case, something that you took for granted no longer holds.

Psychologists sometimes call these life transitions or turning points, and they can be as disorienting as larger events for the person going through them. There's no hierarchy of suffering that decides who is allowed to feel shaken. If your world has shifted, even by what looks small from outside, it's a real shift, and it deserves to be taken seriously.

It's worth saying that the word trauma has a clinical meaning, and that not every painful event meets it. The research on shattered assumptions applies most clearly to events that involve a threat to life or safety. For other hard experiences, the same processes may operate in a milder form. Using the right word is not about ranking pain. It's about choosing the right kind of help.

show.sub: Trauma is a word with limits

segments.say: Four terms from this chapter. Assimilation is fitting a new event into old beliefs. Accommodation is changing the beliefs to fit. Trauma, in the clinical sense, is an event involving threat to life or safety. And a life transition is a major change that disrupts our usual way of living.

show.title: Words to keep from this chapter

segments.say: You can try something gentle with this chapter. Think of a belief you once held with certainty, that later changed. It could be about a person, a place, a career, a faith. Notice what changed it. Notice how it felt in the time in between, when the old view had gone and the new one hadn't formed. And notice what you kept. Most people find that even in big changes, something stayed, such as a value or a loyalty or a way of caring. That thing is part of the thread that carries you from one view of the world to the next. Picture this scene. A woman who was always certain her city was safe is burgled, and over the next few weeks she tries two responses. At first she tells herself that it was a freak event that tells her nothing, and carries on exactly as before. That is assimilation. Then, gradually, she adds a lock, speaks to her neighbours and revises her belief to something like, the city is mostly safe, and I can take sensible care. That is accommodation. Neither response is wrong in itself. Most of us use both, and the skill is in knowing when each one is needed.

show.title: Noticing your own assumptions
items: Think of a belief that was once certain and later changed
Notice how it felt in between

segments.say: A bowl, cracked and mended with seams of gold. The Japanese practice of kintsugi doesn't hide the break. It makes the repair part of the object's story. It's a lovely image for what psychologists describe: a mind that has been broken, and rebuilt in a way that doesn't pretend that nothing happened.

You can hold a broken assumption and a growing new one at the same time. You can grieve what you've lost, and still be rebuilding. The research doesn't ask you to choose one. It suggests that this double state, uncomfortable as it is, is how most people get through.

So what did we learn? That trauma can collide with our deepest assumptions. That people can assimilate an event into old beliefs, or accommodate by changing them. That research supports parts of the theory, and shows it's less all-or-nothing than it sounds. And that smaller breakings count too.
In our next chapter, we'll tackle one of the most famous ideas about loss: the five stages of grief. How well does it hold up when it's tested against real people?
